disease-biology|mouse.summary: Evidence is mixed: some studies find substantial transcriptomic agreement (Takao et al. 2015 Spearman 0.43–0.68 with 77–93% genes directionally concordant; Godec et al. 2016 Spearman 0.857 for leading-edge genes), while others find near-random overlap (Seok et al. 2013 R^2 ≤0.09; Kodamullil et al. 2017: 12% of human-deregulated genes mimicked). Concordance depends on disease, model, pathway/threshold choices and exposure duration.
key_numbers: R^2 ≤ 0.09 — Pearson R^2 human vs mouse orthologs (Seok et al. 2013)
Spearman 0.43–0.68 — rank correlation human vs mouse (Takao et al. 2015)
77–93% — genes changed in same direction (Takao et al. 2015)
12% — human-deregulated genes mimicked by mouse models (Kodamullil et al. 2017)
Recall 0.40 — genes altered in human CLD detected by 12‑month CCl4 mouse model (Holland et al. 2022)
disease-biology|mouse.why_range_is_wide: Results vary by disease/model, choice of gene/pathway subsets and statistical thresholds (e.g. exposure duration, fold‑change cutoffs).

disease-biology|pig.summary: Tarandovskiy et al. 2020: swine thrombin generation partly tracked humans—thrombin peak 242.35 nM vs 484.25 nM and production rate 93.60 vs 111.51 nM/min—but swine had no detectable plasmin. Authors note baboon and rhesus matched humans better and swine resembled rat (swine n=20).
key_numbers: Thrombin peak: 242.35 nM (swine) vs 484.25 nM (human)
Thrombin production rate: 93.60 nM/min (swine) vs 111.51 nM/min (human)
Plasmin: not detected (swine) vs peak 457.20 nM and rate 34.80 nM/min (human)

disease-biology|d. melanogaster.summary: Zong et al. 2023 found modest cross‑species transcriptional concordance: most D. melanogaster–C. elegans within‑stage genome‑wide c‑scores exceeded 0.1. One larva–larva pairing had c‑score 0.087, slightly below the 0.1 threshold.
key_numbers: most within‑stage DM vs CE genome‑wide c‑scores > 0.1
ce.lar–dm.lar c‑score = 0.087

disease-biology|non-human primate.summary: Tarandovskiy et al. 2020: baboon and rhesus thrombin peaks were near human (baboon 433.8 vs 484.3 nM; rhesus 399.0 nM) and thrombin production rates matched human (124.2, 111.2 vs 111.5 nM/min), but plasmin measures were higher. Small samples (n=10–12) and plasmin peaks/production rates exceeded human values (~1.2–2.6×).
key_numbers: Baboon thrombin peak 433.78 nM (human 484.25 nM)
Rhesus thrombin peak 398.95 nM (human 484.25 nM)
Thrombin production rate — baboon 124.22, rhesus 111.22 (human 111.51 nM/min)
Plasmin production rate — baboon 90.81, rhesus 49.78 (human 34.80 nM/min)
disease-biology|non-human primate.why_range_is_wide: Range reflects assay-specific differences: thrombin parameters approximate human values while plasmin parameters are consistently higher, and values differ between baboon and rhesus.

disease-biology|rabbit.summary: Tarandovskiy et al. 2020: rabbit thrombin and plasmin generation were markedly lower than human — thrombin peak 71.6 nM (≈15% of human 484.25) and rate 14.9 nM/min (≈13% of human 111.51); plasmin peak 197.7 nM (≈43% of human 457.20) and rate 17.6 nM/min (≈51% of human 34.80). PG curves were highly variable.
disease-biology|rabbit.direction: evidence does not favour the model
key_numbers: Thrombin peak 71.6 nM (≈15% of human 484.25 nM)
Thrombin production rate 14.93 nM/min (≈13% of human 111.51 nM/min)
Plasmin peak 197.71 nM (≈43% of human 457.20 nM)
Plasmin production rate 17.63 nM/min (≈51% of human 34.80 nM/min)
disease-biology|rabbit.why_range_is_wide: Rabbit plasmin-generation (PG) curves were reported as highly variable.

disease-biology|rat.summary: Evidence is mixed: rats often mirror human disease biology — 26/30 biochemical parameters concordant (7.9% vs 7.3% magnitude; Goutianos et al. 2015) and 50% whole-transcriptome DEG alignment in MASLD (Vacca et al. 2024). But key mismatches occur: 10/19 biomarkers differ with vitamin C (Veskoukis et al. 2016) and lower coagulation peaks in rats (thrombin 270 vs 484 nM; Tarandovskiy et al. 2020).
key_numbers: 26/30 biochemical parameters changed toward same direction after exercise (Goutianos et al. 2015)
7.9% vs 7.3% magnitude of uniform changes (rats vs humans; Goutianos et al. 2015)
50% whole-transcriptome DEG alignment with human MASLD (Vacca et al. 2024)
10/19 biomarkers showed species×vitamin C interactions (Veskoukis et al. 2016)
Rat thrombin peak 270.28 nM vs human 484.25 nM (Tarandovskiy et al. 2020)
disease-biology|rat.why_range_is_wide: Concordance varies by endpoint: good for exercise biomarkers and behavioral measures, but poorer for pharmacologic/vitamin responses, coagulation parameters and some tissue-specific gene-expression profiles.

disease-biology|c. elegans.summary: Zong et al. 2023: C. elegans shows modest cross-species genome-wide concordance for disease biology — most within-stage c-scores exceed 0.1 (the study's 'solid' cutoff), but some pairs are lower (ce.lar–dm.lar = 0.087). Because c-scores are low in absolute terms (~0.1), tracking human inflammatory-disease signals is mixed and limited.
key_numbers: most within-stage genome-wide c-scores >0.1 (study 'solid' cutoff)
example c-score ce.lar–dm.lar = 0.087
disease-biology|c. elegans.why_range_is_wide: Concordance varies by developmental stage pair; some stage-specific comparisons (e.g., ce.lar–dm.lar) fell below the 0.1 threshold.

disease-biology|horse.summary: Oreff et al. 2021: horse tenocytes resembled human migration/wound-closure and gene expression under transient inflammation (Mahalanobis 9.59; tenogenic markers Mahalanobis 6.88; MMPs Mahalanobis 4.65) but differed in baseline proliferation (slope difference 0.30) and inflammatory mediators (Mahalanobis 17.77). Results come from small in vitro replicates (n=3 per species) and similarity depended on inflammatory state.
key_numbers: Mahalanobis 9.59 — all genes, transient inflammation
Mahalanobis 6.88 — tenogenic markers (SCX,TNC,TNMD)
Mahalanobis 4.65 — MMPs (MMP1,MMP3,MMP13)
Proliferation slope 0.3000 — difference to human under healthy conditions
Mahalanobis 17.77 — inflammatory mediators (COX2, IL6)
disease-biology|horse.why_range_is_wide: Similarity changed with inflammation state: Mahalanobis 23.05 (healthy), 9.59 (transient), 12.97 (constant).

efficacy|mouse.summary: Mixed evidence: Spanagel et al. 2017 reports mouse/rat alcohol models yielded three clinically translated drugs (acamprosate, naltrexone, nalmefene) and cross‑species 'incubation' phenomena; Pan et al. 2020 finds mouse TGI poorly predicts approval (AUC 0.45; TGI medians 0.74 vs 0.77, p=0.375). Pan et al. 2020 cautions that few approved drugs and variable TGI measurement limit that analysis.
key_numbers: 3 drugs translated (acamprosate, naltrexone, nalmefene) — Spanagel et al. 2017
AUC 0.45 for TGI predicting success — Pan et al. 2020
TGI medians 0.74 (approved) vs 0.77 (failed) — Pan et al. 2020
p = 0.375 for median TGI difference — Pan et al. 2020

disease-biology|sheep.summary: Sheep tenocyte gene expression best matched human under constant inflammation (Mahalanobis distance 8.94 vs 24.78 in healthy), so sheep track human inflammatory-state profiles but not healthy-state profiles. Results vary by inflammatory condition and use small in vitro samples (3 replicates).
key_numbers: 8.94 — Mahalanobis distance to human (all genes, constant inflammation)
10.62 — Mahalanobis distance to human (all genes, transient inflammation)
24.78 — Mahalanobis distance to human (all genes, healthy)
-0.0878 — proliferation slope difference to human (constant inflammation; p=0.009)
0.018555 — migration slope difference to human (healthy; p=5.46e-05)
disease-biology|sheep.why_range_is_wide: Similarity depends on inflammatory condition: close under constant (8.94) and transient (10.62) inflammation but distant when healthy (24.78).

efficacy|non-human primate.summary: Evidence shows partial concordance: NHPs reproduced human/lab/clinical attenuation of cocaine choice with d‑amphetamine but not with KOR antagonists or buspirone. Female monkeys showed greater cocaine preference than males, with no menstrual/estrous cycle effect.
key_numbers: 1/3 drug classes (d‑amphetamine vs KOR antagonists, buspirone) showed concordant attenuation in NHPs and humans
0/2 KOR antagonists (nor‑BNI, 5′‑guanidonaltrindole) failed to attenuate drug versus food choice in NHPs
0/2 repeated buspirone tests failed to attenuate cocaine or methamphetamine choice in NHPs

efficacy|non-rodent.summary: Leenaars et al. 2019 does not assess efficacy: it reports toxicology concordance for non-rodents — liver-effect concordance 40% (n=951 compounds) and animal data predicted 48% of 221 human adverse drug reactions. No direct efficacy data are provided.
key_numbers: 40% concordance of liver effects between non-rodent species and humans (n=951 compounds)
48% of human adverse drug reactions predicted from animal data (n=221 human toxicity events)

efficacy|sheep.summary: Perel et al. 2007: in sheep (ewe antenatal corticosteroids) pooled neonatal mortality was higher — OR 12.5 (95% CI 1.9–79.2) — so the sheep result contradicted human outcomes. This estimate is imprecise due to sparse ewe data and a wide CI.
efficacy|sheep.direction: evidence does not favour the model
key_numbers: OR 12.5 (95% CI 1.9–79.2) — pooled neonatal mortality in ewe models (antenatal corticosteroids)
efficacy|sheep.why_range_is_wide: Wide confidence interval reflects sparse pooled ewe data and imprecision (few events/studies).

efficacy|rodent.summary: Rodent efficacy sometimes mirrors human outcomes (ACEi/ARB, SGLT2, GLP‑1RA) but overall translation is inconsistent across studies. O'Collins et al. 2006: 62% of focal ischemia animal results were superior to control; Leenaars et al. 2019: 44% rodent–human liver concordance and 48% ADR predictivity; Ritskes‑Hoitinga et al. 2022: translation 0–100% and 82% animal studies positive.
key_numbers: 62% animal focal ischemia results superior to control (O'Collins et al. 2006)
44% rodent–human concordance for liver effects (Leenaars et al. 2019)
48% of adverse drug reactions predictable from animal data (Leenaars et al. 2019)
0–100% translation rates reported (Ritskes‑Hoitinga et al. 2022)
82% of preclinical animal studies reported positive findings (Ritskes‑Hoitinga et al. 2022)
efficacy|rodent.why_range_is_wide: Translation rates vary by intervention, outcome and study/reporting heterogeneity (including publication bias).

safety-pharmacology|dog.summary: Dog data generally track human safety signals: 91% of human QT‑prolonging drugs also prolonged QT in dogs (Valentin et al. 2022), dog QTc AUC=0.81 vs clinical (Pollard et al. 2017), combined BP/HR sensitivity 78% and specificity 79% (Bhatt et al. 2019), and moxifloxacin raised QTc +16.6 ms in dogs vs ~10 ms in humans (Sadko et al. 2024). Concordance varies by endpoint, assay, exposure and drug class (e.g. 31% overall discordance reported; results change when β2‑agonists are excluded).
key_numbers: 91% of human QT‑prolonging drugs also prolonged QT in dogs (Valentin et al. 2022)
AUC = 0.81 for dog QTc vs clinical QTc (Pollard et al. 2017)
Sensitivity 78% and specificity 79% for large-animal to human combined BP/HR (Bhatt et al. 2019)
+16.6 ms QTc in dogs for moxifloxacin vs ~10 ms in humans (Sadko et al. 2024)
safety-pharmacology|dog.why_range_is_wide: Varies by endpoint (QT vs BP/HR), assay type, exposure multiples and drug-class exclusions (e.g. β2‑agonists).

efficacy|rat.summary: Spanagel et al. 2017 and Banks et al. 2017 find rat efficacy models partly track human outcomes: Spanagel reports three alcoholism drugs translated (acamprosate, naltrexone, nalmefene) and matching phenomena (incubation; withdrawal hyperglutamatergic activity). Banks shows drug-vs-food choice predicts some drugs (d‑amphetamine) but not others (KOR antagonists, buspirone); sex differences also aligned.
key_numbers: 3 alcoholism drugs translated (acamprosate, naltrexone, nalmefene) — Spanagel et al. 2017
Incubation of drug seeking replicated in humans (smokers, alcoholics, cocaine addicts) — Spanagel et al. 2017
Withdrawal hyperglutamatergic activity matched rats and humans — Spanagel et al. 2017
Drug-vs-food choice predicted some drugs (d‑amphetamine) but not KOR antagonists or buspirone — Banks et al. 2017
Sex differences in cocaine vs food choice observed in rats and humans — Banks et al. 2017
efficacy|rat.why_range_is_wide: Translation varies by drug class and endpoint: some pharmacotherapies and neural/behavioural findings translate, while others (e.g., KOR antagonists, CRH‑R1 antagonists) fail.

safety-pharmacology|rat.summary: Bhatt et al. 2019: Rat results matched large-animal combined BP+HR changes reasonably (sensitivity 84%, specificity 71%; PPV 90%, NPV 60%) but were weaker for single endpoints (BP specificity 59%, HR sensitivity 64%). Direction of change mismatched in ~23–26% and PPV/NPV depend on dataset prevalence.
key_numbers: 84% sensitivity (rat→large animal, combined BP+HR)
71% specificity (rat→large animal, combined BP+HR)
90% PPV (rat→large animal, combined BP+HR)
60% NPV (rat→large animal, combined BP+HR)
23–26% opposite direction of change (HR 23%, BP 26%)
safety-pharmacology|rat.why_range_is_wide: Concordance differs by analysis: combined BP+HR agreement is higher than BP-only or HR-only, and directionality varies by endpoint.

toxicology|dog.summary: Dog toxicology is inconsistent: lack of dog toxicity often corresponds to lack of human toxicity (NPVs up to ~95%; 72% probability no human toxicity if dog shows none). However dogs' ability to predict human adverse events is limited (median PPV ≈0.67; iNLR 1.10).
key_numbers: 72% probability no human toxicity given no dog toxicity (Bailey et al. 2019)
NPVs up to ~95% for many organ classes (Monticello et al. 2017)
median PPV ≈0.67 for dog (Atkins et al. 2020)
dog iNLR 1.10 (Bailey et al. 2015)
dog cardiac LR+ 6.11 (Clark et al. 2018)
toxicology|dog.why_range_is_wide: Results vary by organ/endpoint, dataset and study design (e.g., high organ-specific NPVs vs lower overall PPV and selection biases).

toxicology|mouse.summary: Evidence is mixed: overall mouse findings only weakly track human toxicity — Atkins et al. 2020 reports median PPV 0.57 and NPV 0.57 (all grades) and Bailey et al. 2015 reports mouse iNLR 1.39 (≈1). However, Clark et al. 2018 found moderate LR+ for cardiac (5.29) and hepatobiliary (3.73) endpoints.
key_numbers: median PPV 0.57 (mouse, all toxicity grades, Atkins et al. 2020)
median NPV 0.57 (mouse, all toxicity grades, Atkins et al. 2020)
mouse iNLR 1.39 (Bailey et al. 2015)
LR+ 5.29 (mouse, cardiac disorders, Clark et al. 2018)
LR+ 3.73 (mouse, hepatobiliary disorders, Clark et al. 2018)
toxicology|mouse.why_range_is_wide: Metrics vary by endpoint and severity (e.g., PPV 0.43–0.57 and NPV 0.57–0.81 across toxicity grades; LR+ differs by organ system).

toxicology|rabbit.summary: Evidence is mixed: rabbit results track some human toxicities (QT post-test odds 83%; LR+ cardiac 3.54; LR+ hepatobiliary 2.8 — Clark et al. 2018) but other analyses find little evidential value. Bailey et al. 2015 reports median rabbit iNLR 1.12, near unity.
key_numbers: 83% post-test odds for QT prolongation (rabbit, Clark et al. 2018)
LR+ 3.54 for cardiac disorders (rabbit, Clark et al. 2018)
LR+ 2.8 for hepatobiliary disorders (rabbit, Clark et al. 2018)
Median iNLR 1.12 (rabbit, Bailey et al. 2015)
toxicology|rabbit.why_range_is_wide: Concordance differs by endpoint and dataset: cardiac/QT signals are stronger while overall/selectivity and absence-of-toxicity metrics are weak or near unity.

toxicology|rodent.summary: Monticello et al. 2017: rodents showed moderate sensitivity (48%) but low overall PPV (43%), while specificity was 84% and NPV 86% — rodents often ruled out human adverse effects but less reliably predicted them. Performance varied by organ (PPV 0%–54%; e.g. 0% ophthalmology, 54% biochemical).
key_numbers: 48% sensitivity (detected human adverse effects)
43% PPV (rodent positives matching human AEs)
84% specificity (correctly predicted absence of human AEs)
86% NPV (rodent negatives matching absence in humans)
PPV range 0%–54% across organ systems
toxicology|rodent.why_range_is_wide: Variation reflects different organ systems (e.g., PPV 0% ophthalmology to 54% biochemical; NPV 14% 'other' to 96% renal/ophthalmology).

toxicology|non-human primate.summary: Evidence is mixed: NHPs can strongly predict some human toxicities (Clark et al. 2018: cynomolgus LR+ 9.52 cardiac, 11.02 hepatobiliary; Monticello et al. 2017: PPV 83% for nervous system). But overall predictive power is modest (PPV/sensitivity ≈43–72%, NPV/specificity ≈50–86%; iNLR ≈1.02; no‑toxicity given no NHP finding ≈70%).
key_numbers: LR+ 9.52 (cynomolgus, cardiac; Clark et al. 2018)
LR+ 11.02 (cynomolgus, hepatobiliary; Clark et al. 2018)
PPV 83% (nervous system; Monticello et al. 2017)
Overall PPV/sensitivity 43–72% (across studies)
iNLR 1.02 (NHP-human median; Bailey et al. 2015)
toxicology|non-human primate.why_range_is_wide: Variation stems from differences by organ class, toxicity grade and study dataset—some endpoints show high concordance while aggregated measures are low.

toxicology|rat.summary: Mixed evidence: some rat data show modest prediction—Atkins et al. median PPV 0.65 (all toxicities) and Clark et al. LR+ 4.73 (cardiac), 2.74 (hepatobiliary)—but others find little evidential weight (Bailey et al. rat iNLR 1.82; Atkins NPV 0.51). Jang et al.'s 71% pools rats+dogs and varies by endpoint.
key_numbers: PPV 0.65 (median, rat, all toxicity grades; Atkins et al. 2020)
NPV 0.51 (median, rat, all toxicity grades; Atkins et al. 2020)
LR+ 4.73 (rat, cardiac; Clark et al. 2018)
LR+ 2.74 (rat, hepatobiliary; Clark et al. 2018)
iNLR 1.82 (rat-human median; Bailey et al. 2015)
toxicology|rat.why_range_is_wide: Concordance varies by endpoint and toxicity grade; some endpoints (e.g., cardiac/QT) show higher rat–human agreement while others and severe toxicities show lower or inconsistent predictive value.

veterinary|dog.summary: Mixed evidence: Daluwatumulle et al. 2026 found canine cancer model robustness scores spanning 31–85% (many cancer types >70%), indicating good concordance for several indications. But Petersen-Jones et al. 2015 showed dogs regained near-normal ERG/vision after RPE65 therapy while humans had no ERG improvement and remained visually impaired.
key_numbers: 31–85% model robustness scores across cancers (Daluwatumulle et al. 2026)
many cancer types >70% (several adult/pediatric cancers)
85.05% (adult bladder cancer, Daluwatumulle et al. 2026)
31.1% (adult adrenocortical carcinoma, Daluwatumulle et al. 2026)
Dogs: near-normal ERG vs humans: no ERG change (Petersen-Jones et al. 2015)
veterinary|dog.why_range_is_wide: Scores vary by cancer type and include high-scoring positives (e.g. bladder 85%) and low-scoring negative controls (e.g. ACC ~31%).

safety-pharmacology|non-human primate.summary: Sadko et al. 2024: NHP QTc matched humans (moxifloxacin 10.9 ms in NHP vs ~10 ms in humans) and AQTc slopes were similar (NHP 0.0043 vs human 0.0031 ms/ng/mL). Bhatt et al. 2019: large-animal→human concordance for combined BP/HR ~78% sensitivity/79% specificity but HR sensitivity was 54% (PPV depends on prevalence).
key_numbers: 10.9 ms — QTc increase in NHP (moxifloxacin)
10 ms — QTc change in humans (reference)
0.0043 ms/ng/mL — NHP AQTc slope
0.0031 ms/ng/mL — human AQTc slope
78% sensitivity, 79% specificity — large-animal→human (combined BP/HR); HR sensitivity 54%

toxicology|zebrafish.summary: Zebrafish toxicology generally tracks mammalian outcomes: Cornet et al. 2017 overall accuracy 78% (specificity 89%, sensitivity 68%); McGrath et al. 2008 100% teratogen detection, 75% correct non‑teratogen; Nikam et al. 2020 100% concordance overall/hepatotoxicity, 90% teratogenicity. But concordance varies by endpoint—specificities 77–100% and sensitivities 54–80%, so some toxicities give false negatives.
key_numbers: 78% overall accuracy (Cornet et al. 2017)
89% specificity overall (Cornet et al. 2017)
68% sensitivity overall (Cornet et al. 2017)
100% teratogen detection (McGrath et al. 2008)
100% concordance overall and for hepatotoxicity (Nikam et al. 2020)
toxicology|zebrafish.why_range_is_wide: Variation stems from different toxicity endpoints and assays (neuro/cardio/hepato), which show sensitivities 54–80% and specificities 77–100%.
